rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purification of the body is included even more plainly in the command to purify one’s garments.
rows.anchor: والطهارة لجسده بالأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to purify follows the command to magnify the Lord because purification is prescribed for prayer.
rows.anchor: لأنه لما أمر بالصلاة أمر بالتطهر لها لأن الطهارة مشروعة للصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the Qur’an’s only mention of garment purification under one possible interpretation, while the Prophet is also commanded to purify himself.
rows.anchor: ليس في القرآن ذكر طهارة الثوب إلا في هذه الآية في أحد محاملها وهو مأمور بتزكية نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The combined metonymic and figurative sense best suits the prophetic office; Arabic idiom also calls a person pure of garments.
rows.anchor: والمعنى المركب من الكنائي والمجازي هو الأعلق بإضافة النبوءة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom of being pure of garments is illustrated by lines from Ghaylan al-Thaqafi and Abu Kabsha, attributed to Imruʾ al-Qays.
rows.anchor: وقال غيلان بن سلمة الثقفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ on the command to purify echoes the fāʾ previously discussed in the command to magnify God.
rows.anchor: ودخول الفاء على فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Putting garments before the verb gives special emphasis to them in the command to purify.
rows.anchor: للاهتمام به في الأمر بالتطهير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause may be treated as a fresh sentence, with a pause at kallā.
rows.anchor: مستأنفة ويكون الوقف عند قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAnīd means intensely obstinate and opposed to what is right, from a verb for disputing clear truth.
rows.anchor: الشديد العناد وهو المخالفة للصواب وهو فعيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His obstinacy was his effort to discredit the Qur’an as magic, poetry, or soothsaying despite knowing it was none of these.
rows.anchor: هو محاولته الطعن في القرآن وتحيله للتمويه بأنه سحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat is parenthetical between the account of his obstinacy and his thought, hastening warning for his distress and comfort for the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قصد بهذا الاعتراض تعجيل الوعيد له مساءة له وتعجيل المسرة للنبيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His thinking and devising explains and completes the statement that he was obstinate toward God’s signs.
rows.anchor: عنيدا فهي تكملة وتبيين لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Irhāq means exhausting someone and burdening him with what he cannot bear.
rows.anchor: الإتعاب وتحميل ما لا يطاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaʿūd is a steep, arduous ascent; its intensive form describes an unusually difficult hill, figuratively called ascending.
rows.anchor: العقبة الشديدة التصعد الشاقة على الماشي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase pictures his reversal from ease to misery, beginning with worldly distress and ending in painful afterlife punishment, against his former prosperity.
rows.anchor: أي سينقلب حاله من حال راحة وتنعم إلى حالة سوأى في الدنيا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reported view says his death agony was prolonged: his breath repeatedly rose, but he did not die, foreshadowing the Fire’s punishment.
rows.anchor: طال به النزع فكانت تتصاعد نفسه ثم لا يموت

words: فَقَالَ إِنْ هَٰذَآ إِلَّا سِحْرٌۭ يُؤْثَرُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly threat follows his worldly motives of leadership and envy; the threat of Hell follows his attacks on the Qur’an and denial of revelation.
rows.anchor: وقد وزع وعيده على ما تقتضيه أعماله فإنه لما ذكر عناده وهو من مقاصده السيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The curse is an inserted exclamation between his devising and looking, branching into condemnation because his conduct warrants anger.
rows.anchor: وهو إنشاء شتم مفرع على الإخبار عنه بأنه فكر وقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An interjected sentence can begin with fāʾ: interruption describes its placement, while the fāʾ still connects its meaning; the contrary grammatical objection is mistaken.
rows.anchor: والتفريع لا ينافي الاعتراض لأن الاعتراض وضع الكلام بين كلامين متصلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qutila invokes a killer against him, wishing an end to his wretched life; the formula became a conventional expression of amazement or pity.
rows.anchor: دعاء عليه بأن يقتله قاتل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads the curse as a metonym for reaching a degree that makes the speaker envy him and wish him dead.
rows.anchor: وجعله الزمخشري كناية عن كونه بلغ مبلغا يحسده عليه المتكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects the envy reading: the phrase simply expresses amazement, and here condemns a conclusion that contradicted the man’s earlier denial that the Qur’an was magic.
rows.anchor: وأنا أحسب أن معنى الحسد غير ملحوظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The successive actions coordinate with “devised”; the sequence is a rise in rank, not time, because all occurred during his thinking and planning.
rows.anchor: وهي ارتقاء متوالل فيما اقتضى التعجيب من حاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He looked with his eyes at those present, seeking their opinions about what label to invent for the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: نظر في وجوه الحاضرين يستخرج آراءهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbasa means that he furrowed his face when he could not find an acceptable fault to allege against the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: قطب وجهه لما استعصى عليه ما يصف به القرآن ولم يجد مغمزا مقبولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basara means his face became grim and his color changed from anxiety and frustration at finding no rationally persuasive attack on the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: معناه كلح وجهه وتغير لونه خوفا وكمدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible metaphor is that he abandoned his effort to devise a description for the Qur’an in despair, then turned to arrogant disdain.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون مستعارا لتغيير التفكير الذي كان يفكره ويقدره يأسا من أن يجد ما فكر في انتحاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “turned away” may mean that he increasingly rejected belief in the Prophet, as Pharaoh is described turning away.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون مستعارا لزيادة إعراضه عن تصديق النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The successive expressions satirically portray al-Walīd’s contortions as he strained to invent a description for the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وصفت أشكاله التي تشكل بها لما أجهد نفسه

words: فَقَالَ إِنْ هَٰذَآ إِلَّا سِحْرٌۭ يُؤْثَرُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exclusive wording presents magic as the conclusion of his testing and sorting through possible descriptions of the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: مشعرة بأن استقراء أحوال القرآن بعد السبر والتقسيم أنتج له أنه من قبيل السحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʾthūr means transmitted from ancient people; he calls the magic inherited to answer the objection that its language and effects resemble neither familiar magic nor the Prophet’s state.
rows.anchor: ووصف هذا السحر بأنه مأثور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He alleges that the Qur’an consists of unfamiliar magical sayings to explain its difference from ordinary spells and the Prophet’s circumstances.
rows.anchor: فزعم أنه أقوال سحرية غير مألوفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that it is human speech is an appositive elaboration of the claim that it is magic, since magic can consist of words and deeds.
rows.anchor: بأن السحر يكون أقوالا وأفعالا فهذا من السحر القولي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling it human speech is the conclusion of his allegations: his aim is to deny that the Qur’an is revelation from God.
rows.anchor: مقصوده من ذلك كله أن القرآن ليس وحيا من الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative “what is Saqar?” is fronted from “Saqar, what?” because interrogative mā must lead the sentence.
rows.anchor: لأنه اسم استفهام وله الصدارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first mā is interrogative meaning “what will make you know”; the second is the interrogative predicate of Saqar.
rows.anchor: فإن { ما } الأولى استفهامية . والمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “It leaves nothing” elaborates the terror of “what is Saqar?” and serves as another predicate of Saqar.
rows.anchor: من أهوالها أنها تهلك كل من يصلاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of “leaves nothing” is omitted to make the scope universal: it leaves no one or no part of their bodies.
rows.anchor: أي لا تبقي منهم أحدا أو لا تبقي من أجزائهم شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Nor leaves” coordinates with “leaves nothing” and has the force of a circumstantial clause.
rows.anchor: فهي في معنى الحال ، ومعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqar does not leave anyone cast into it free from its torment; this implies that life is restored after destruction.
rows.anchor: أي لا تتركه غير مصلي بعذابها . وهذه كناية عن إعادة حياته بعد إهلاكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lawwāḥa is a third predicate of Saqar, derived from lawḥ, alteration of a person’s substance through pain.
rows.anchor: من اللوح وهو تغيير الذات من ألمم ونحوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited, unidentified poet uses lāḥa in a line about the scorching winds changing the traveler.
rows.anchor: تقول ما لاحك يا مسافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bashar may mean human skin, whose color the Fire turns black, or collectively denote people without a singular of the same form.
rows.anchor: تغير ألوان الجلود فتجعلها سودا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In gardens” may attach to “they ask one another,” placed first for emphasis; “asking” is then a circumstantial clause about the people of the right.
rows.anchor: حال من { أصحاب اليمين } وهو مناط التفصيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “in gardens” completes an omitted “they are in gardens,” an explanatory resumption; “asking” is circumstantial of the omitted pronoun.
rows.anchor: والجملة استئناف بياني لمضمون جملة الاستثناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reciprocal form can mean the people of the right ask one another about the sinners, with “what put you in Saqar?” explaining their question.
rows.anchor: للدلالة على صدور الفعل من جانبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address in “what put you in Saqar?” implies an omitted questioner: they ask the sinners, rather than the pronoun marking a grammatical shift.
rows.anchor: والتقدير : فيسألون المجرمين ما سلككم في سقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, some of those questioned may tell their companions what they said in answer to the questioners.
rows.anchor: أو يقول بعض المسؤولين لأصحابهم جوابا لسائليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural reciprocal form can instead express repeated questioning or many questioners, rather than an exchange between two sides.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون صيغة التفاعل مستعملة في معنى تكرير الفعل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari compares the form to collective usage such as “we called one another”: multiple people act from one side, not reciprocally.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري في تفسير قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari gives singular “I called” versus plural “we called,” with analogous collective forms for throwing and seeing the moon.
rows.anchor: رميته وتراميناه ورأيت الهلال وتراءيناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the collective reading, the object is omitted and recoverable from the mention of the criminals: they ask about why the criminals entered Saqar.
rows.anchor: والتقدير : يتساءلون المجرمين عنهم ، أي عن سبب حصولهم في سقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salaka originally means to insert something among the parts of another thing, as threading beads; here it metaphorically means thrusting them into Saqar.
rows.anchor: وأصل معنى سلكه أدخله بين أجزاء شيء حقيقة ومنه جاء سلك العقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ makes the denial of intercession follow from each soul being held for what it earned: they remain confined in Saqar.
rows.anchor: فهم دائمون في الارتهان في سقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next passage expresses amazement at their persistence in rejecting reminders, following the statement that the Qur’an is a reminder for humankind.
rows.anchor: تفريع للتعجيب من إصرارهم على الإعراض عن ما فيه تذكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit noun “reminder,” rather than a pronoun, makes the rebuke cover their rejection of every reminder, especially the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وجيء باسم التذكرة الظاهر دون أن يؤتى بضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What is the matter with them?” is an interrogative used to express amazement at their strange state.
rows.anchor: استفهام مستعمل في التعجيب من غرابة حالهم بحيث تجدر أن يستفهم عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “To them” predicates the interrogative mā, with an understood “is established”; muʿriḍīn is a circumstantial clause for its pronoun, and “from the reminder” modifies it.
rows.anchor: والتقدير : ما ثبت لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their imagined rejection is likened to the flight of frightened wild asses, making an abstract state vivid through a sensory comparison.
rows.anchor: وشبهت حالة إعراضهم المتخيلة بحالة فرار حمر نافرة مما ينفرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥumur here are wild donkeys, which startle and flee when they hear a hunter.
rows.anchor: وهو الحمار الوحشي ، وهو شديد النفار إذا أحس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Labīd compares his mount’s speed to a wild animal pursued by a hunter; such flight imagery is common in pre-Islamic and Islamic Arabic poetry.
rows.anchor: كما قال لبيد في تشبيه راحلته في سرعة سيرها بوحشية لحقها الصياد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes this motif in the Muʿallaqāt of Ṭarafa, Labīd, and al-Ḥārith, in rajaz poetry by al-Ḥajjāj and his son, and in Dhū al-Rumma.
rows.anchor: كما في معلقة طرفة ، ومعلقة لبيد ، ومعلقة الحارث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sīn and tāʾ intensify the description: the asses are strongly alarmed and running at full speed.
rows.anchor: للمبالغة في الوصف مثل : استكمل واستجاب

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: These readers pronounce the fāʾ open, taking the word as passive causative: a frightener has startled them; the next phrase specifies the cause.
rows.anchor: بفتح الفاء ، أي استنفرها مستنفر

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read the fāʾ with kasra, meaning that the asses themselves take fright; “they fled from a hunter” explains their alarm.
rows.anchor: بكسر الفاء ، أي استنفرت هي مثل : استجاب

rows.speaker: محمد بن سلام
rows.claim: In a report preserved by al-Rāzī, Muḥammad ibn Sallām asks the eloquent Bedouin Abū Sawwār about the phrase; the Bedouin shifts from fatḥ to kasr after hearing that the asses fled.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن سلام : سألت أبا سوار الغنوي وكان أعرابيا فصيحا

rows.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes, including Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and Mujāhid, take qaswara as a collective noun for archers, or as an irregular plural; this follows the familiar Arab simile.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وعكرمة ومجاهد وغيرهم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة وزيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Another transmitted view takes qaswara as a singular meaning lion.
rows.anchor: وهذا مروي عن أبي هريرة وزيد بن أسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also glosses it as lion in Ethiopic; his differing statements may be verbal, since he denied that lion is the word’s original Arabic sense.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس : إنه الأسد بالحبشية

rows.speaker: ابن السبكي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Subkī lists qaswara among Qur’anic words from a language other than Arabic.
rows.anchor: وقد عده ابن السبكي في الألفاظ الواردة في القرآن بغير لغة العرب

rows.speaker: ابن سيده
rows.claim: Ibn Sīda says both qaswar and qaswara mean lion, with the latter grammatically feminine like Usāma.
rows.anchor: القسور الأسد والقسورة كذلك ، أنثوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If qaswara means lion, the simile is novel: their rejection mixes with terror inspired by the Qur’an’s menacing warnings, combining two representations.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا فهو تشبيه مبتكر لحالة إعراض مخلوط برعب مما تضمنته قوارع القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaswara is chosen because it works for both proposed similes and preserves the verse ending.
rows.anchor: هنا لصلاحيته للتشبيهين مع الرعاية على الفاصلة

words: بَلْ يُرِيدُ كُلُّ ٱمْرِئٍۢ مِّنْهُمْ أَن يُؤْتَىٰ صُحُفًۭا مُّنَشَّرَةًۭ
rows.speaker: أبو جهل وعبد الله بن أبي أمية
rows.claim: Abū Jahl, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Umayya, and other Quraysh unbelievers demanded a personal document from God addressed to each man, as another tactic for denying revelation.
rows.anchor: إضراب انتقالي لذكر حالة أخرى من أحوال عنادهم إذ قال أبو جهل وعبد الله بن أبي أمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural may mean that every command or prohibition for each person would need its own separate document.
rows.anchor: إما لأنهم سألوا أن يكون كل أمر أو نهي تأتي الواحد منهم في شأنه صحيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, because they jointly demanded a named document for each man, the collection is described as if all those documents came to every individual.
rows.anchor: وإما لأنهم لما سألوا أن تأتي كل واحد منهم صحيفة باسمه وكانوا جماعة متفقين جمع لذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Munashshara means unrolled, open, and readable; they reject a folded document whose contents they cannot see, and the intensive form stresses its being unfolded.
rows.anchor: أي لا نكتفي بصحيفة مطوية لا نعلم ما كتب فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites the report about the stoning to show the verb’s use: they opened the Torah.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث الرجم فنشروا التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kallā rejects and rebukes the apparent demand: they will not receive such documents.
rows.anchor: وردع عن ذلك ، أي لا يكون لهم ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transition rejects another claim: their demand is only evasion, since they would not believe even if given a document; they do not fear the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ثم أضرب على كلامهم بإبطال آخر بحرف الإضراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their lack of fear is a metonym for disbelief in the afterlife; denial of resurrection underlies their rejection of the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: أي لا يؤمنون بها فكني عن عدم الإيمان بالآخرة بعدم الخوف منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second kallā reinforces the rebuke: they will not receive individual scrolls; the Qur’an alone admonishes them.
rows.anchor: لا يؤتون صحفا منشورة ولا يوزعون إلا بالقرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that it is a reminder explains why their demand for scrolls is rejected; the pronoun refers to the Qur’an, and the indefinite noun magnifies it.
rows.anchor: بأن هذا القرآن تذكرة عظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The response parallels the answer to those who demanded signs: the Qur’an being recited is sufficient as mercy and reminder for believers.
rows.anchor: قل إنما الآيات عند الله وإنما أنا نذير مبين أو لم يكفهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whoever wishes may remember” follows naturally from calling the Qur’an a reminder and resembles the corresponding line in Sūrat al-Muzzammil.
rows.anchor: تفريع على أنه تذكرة ونظيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to the Qur’an, with the construction understood as “remember by it.”
rows.anchor: وهو القرآن فيكون على الحذف والإيصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the pronoun may refer to God, understood from context despite no prior mention of His name in these verses.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يعود إلى الله تعالى وإن لم يتقدم لاسمه ذكر في هذه الآيات لأنه مستحضر من المقام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whoever wishes” means whoever wants to take heed may do so through the Qur’an; this invites willing reflection and warns that neglect has no excuse.
rows.anchor: أي من أراد أن يتذكر ذكر بالقرآن وهو مثل قوله آنفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People possess a will that grounds religious duties and reward or punishment, while their act of remembering remains conditioned on God’s will.
rows.anchor: لا يقع إلا مشروطا بمشيئة الله أن يتذكروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashʿarī theologians call the human will relevant to accountability kasb, while Muʿtazilites call it created capacity; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the formulations are close.
rows.anchor: وعند المعتزلة بالقدرة الحادثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s supreme will cannot be resisted or compelled; without its attachment to a servant’s will, the servant does not attain what he wants.
rows.anchor: المشيئة العظمى التي لا يمانعها مانع ولا يقسرها قاسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When divine will enables obedience and fulfillment of God’s commands, it is called tawfīq.
rows.anchor: وهذه المشيئة هي المعبر عنها بالتوفيق إذا تعلقت بإقدار العبد على الداعية إلى الطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When divine will leaves someone to the misguidance of corrupt ideas and desires, it is called khidhlān.
rows.anchor: وبالخذلان إذا تعلقت بتركه في ضلاله الذي أوبقته فيه آراؤه الضالة وشهواته الخبيثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When divine will rescues someone from error and illuminates the path of good, it is called luṭf; ʿUmar’s conversion after opposition is an example.
rows.anchor: وإذا تعلقت بانتشال العبد من أوحال الضلال وبإنارة سبيل الخير لبصيرته سميت لطفا مثل تعلقها بإيمان عمر بن الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of God’s guidance and misguidance corresponds to the verse describing God opening or constricting a person’s breast.
rows.anchor: فمن يرد الله أن يهديه يشرح صدره للإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr reconciles God’s command with accountability for error through the discussion in 4:78–79, while noting a divine mystery hidden behind promises and warnings.
rows.anchor: هذا حاصل ما يتمخض من الجمع بين أدلة الشريعة المقتضية أن الأمر لله

rows.speaker: نافع ويعقوب
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Yaʿqūb read the verb with second-person tāʾ, turning to address the hearers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع ويعقوب { وما تذكرون } بمثناة فوقية على الالتفات

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read with third-person yāʾ; Ibn ʿĀshūr explains that they generally fail to heed unless God grants enabling and grace.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى أنهم يغلب عليهم الاستمرار على عدم الذكرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God grants enabling to those who believed before the verse was revealed and to those who believed afterward.
rows.anchor: وقد شاء الله ذلك فيمن آمنوا قبل نزول هذه الآية ومن آمنوا بعد نزولها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing statement explains the invitation to remember: remembrance leads to piety, so people should remember and fear God, who alone merits that fear.
rows.anchor: تقوية للتعريض بالترغيب في التذكر والتذكر يفضي إلى التقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Definiteness in both parts of “He is worthy of piety” restricts the right to be feared and obeyed to God alone.
rows.anchor: يفيد قصر مستحق اتقاء العباد إياه على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening with an oath signals that what follows is important and prompts the listener’s anticipation.
rows.anchor: افتتاح السورة بالقسم مؤذن بأن ما سيذكر بعده أمر مهم لتستشرف به نفس السامع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Swearing by the Day of Resurrection is an apt prelude, since the sūra’s purpose is to depict that Day.
rows.anchor: وكون القسم بيوم القيامة براعة استهلال لأن غرض السورة وصف بيوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath’s subject is itself among the realities whose states are affirmed, raising its status for the one swearing, as in Abū Tammām’s poetic comparison.
rows.anchor: كون المقسم به هو المقسم على أحواله تنبيها على زيادة مكانته عند المقسم كقول أبي تمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I do not swear” is still an oath: the negation feigns restraint from swearing by something so sacred and implies that nothing is dearer to swear by.
rows.anchor: لقصد المبالغة في تحقيق حرمة المقسم به بحيث يوهم للسامع
